newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE -Albanian traffic of hope flows after pyramid scam.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE -Albanian traffic of hope flows after pyramid scam.

text.p: Drugs and illegal emigrants are Albania's two biggest exports and trade in both is thriving in this dilapidated southern port city.

Thousands of Albanians pinned their dreams for prosperity on risky pyramid investment funds but now many of these schemes have failed, people in Europe's poorest country are looking abroad for salvation.
"A lot of marijuana is building up at the moment. People have bought new power boats and are shipping it off to Italy," said a policeman, who declined to be named.

Locals report that the number of young men eager to flee grinding poverty in Albania and escape to nearby Italy and Greece has also increased since the start of the year when the infamous pyramids began to tumble.

A middle-aged man, who operates one of six high-speed motor boats that currently ply the narrow stretch of sea between the heel of Italy and Vlore, said about 100 people a night were making the illegal crossing.
"We're not bad, we're just giving people a chance to travel freely," he said. "It's crucial to us, an industry without smoke."

Signs that the illegal business is bearing fruit are clear to see around Vlore, with flashy buildings popping up on around the coast -- a stark contrast to the shabby breeze-block houses built under the old communist government.
The latest Mercedes and BMW cars, most stolen from Germany and Italy, also cruise the potholed streets.
ILLEGAL EXODUS ALARMS NEIGHBOURS

An estimated 500,000 Albanians live abroad, most of them illegally, with neighbouring Greece the favourite destination. The Greek authorities arrested and deported some 1.15 million Albanians between 1991 and mid-1996.
However Italy, just 40 nautical miles away, also acts as a magnet for Albanians. Many watch Italian television and are drawn by the images of comfortable living.
The flow of clandestini, as the illegal emigrants are known, started when Albania's hardline Stalinist government was ousted in 1990 after more than four decades of repression.
The traffic grew to epidemic proportions early last year, forcing Albanian President Sali Berisha to intervene on the insistence of an exasperated Italian government.
The police presence in this litter-strewn Adriatic port was swiftly beefed up, many speed boats were impounded and the night-time dash to Italy virtually halted.

Most of the seized boats were small inflatables, which can easily outpace the more cumbersome naval vessels which patrol the Albanian and Italian coastline, but one huge power launch capable of carrying 60 people was also taken.
"When this was loaded up with drugs and clandestini the captain was making $100,000 a night," the police officer said. "My salary is $100 a month."
The number of police around Vlore thinned in January, as officers were redeployed elsewhere in this small Balkan state in the wake of rioting sparked by the pyramid scandal.
Taking advantage of reduced security and spurred on by the worry of life without the high-yielding pyramids, young people are again coming to the port to seek a passage.
Many teenage girls are also taken across the Adriatic where they invariably end up as prostitutes, controlled by ruthless gangs of Albanian pimps who operate throughout Italy.
Some young women are duped into going in the hope that they will find work as domestics. Others are taken from their homes by force and treated little better than slaves.
FAMILIES DEPEND ON REMITTANCES FROM ABROAD
Five years after the birth of democracy, the expectations of well-being that came with it remain as distant as ever in Albania which still relies heavily on the rural economy.
Analysts believe more than $1 billion is tied up in the pyramid schemes and with regular interest payments now halted, families will rely on remittances from migrants more than ever.
The middle-aged man who organises the trips, himself a former clandestini who worked for more than three years in Italy, charges people around $400 for the 2-1/2 hour journey.
His boat, which holds 23 people, heads for beaches close to the Italian port of Brindisi. Once there, a guide puts them in contact with underground networks which find the Albanians work.
"My family has lost everything in the pyramids...I have to go abroad and start sending money home," said one youth who aimed to go to Florence, where his uncle was already working.
Banking officials say that between $350-450 million was sent back to Albania by its army of migrants in 1996 against a gross domestic product worth a little under $2.5 billion.

No-one knows how much money was made by the drug trade, but a senior financial source said locally-grown marijuana was bringing millions of dollars to the desperately underdeveloped local economy. Heroin from Turkey and Macedonia was also being shifted to Italy via Albania.
"Illegal immigration and drug money are by far and away the largest source of revenue for Albania," said a financial consultant who advises the World Bank, declining to be named.

One 17-year-old said he and three friends took about 100 kg (220 lb) of marijuana to the southern Italian city of Lecce last month. They were each paid $600 for the two-day mission, compared with an average monthly wage in Albania of $65.
The street value of 100 kg of marijuana is around $900,000.
"It was easy," the teenager said. "An Italian met me in Lecce, took the bag and that was that. It is very well organised," he added. He returned home by ferry.

With no other industry worth speaking of in the area, locals see no harm in the clandestini trade, arguing that millions of Italians and Greeks did the same 100 years ago when they went to the United States and Australia to find wealth.
"They did it, now it's our turn," said an engineer called Aristidh, whose brother works in Greece.
